note: ATV2 batch b7 option layer, authored before world selection.

pivots.stem: According to the professor, what did the Cauwenbroek estate ledgers show about plantings of the Groenvelder vine?
settings: New plantings came in one short burst, with little added in the decades that followed
The vine spread plot by plot across two generations, replacing older varieties a few rows at a time
It went in first on the poorer slopes and moved onto the better ground later
It stayed a minor planting, kept mainly for blending with the estate's established varieties

pivots.stem: Why does the professor bring up the printed pruning manual from Tervoss?
settings: Its diagrams differ from local usage in a detail that helps trace where growers learned the technique
Its late date suggests print followed the practice around the region rather than carrying it
Its author complains that growers ignored written instruction, a remark the professor finds revealing
It preserves a name for the technique that the spoken dialect had by then dropped

pivots.stem: What is the professor's position on Doorslaeghe's claim that the arched-cane training arrived in Malderwyck with seasonal pruning crews?
settings: He accepts it for the earliest vineyards, on the strength of the parish hiring records
He accepts the broad picture but thinks the crews came from a different district than Doorslaeghe names
He argues the timing runs the wrong way, with the crews arriving after the method was in place
He thinks the landlords drove the change, pointing to clauses that begin appearing in the leases

pivots.stem: What does the professor suggest the terrace survey team is likely to do next?
settings: Extend the mapping into the neighboring valley, where older terraces are said to survive
Compare the terrace walls against dated examples elsewhere, to put rough ages on the local ones
Revisit plots named in the estate records, to see whether the old row spacing can still be traced
Publish the measurements, so growers in other districts can report terraces matching the local pattern

pivots.stem: What is the professor's main point about why the Vroestel and Karnhout offices' baseline measurements disagreed?
settings: The rods responded differently to temperature, and the corrections in use did not capture the difference
The offices reduced their raw readings by different procedures, so the gap arose on paper rather than in the field
Ground conditions at the two sites unsettled the apparatus in ways that told on the results
The offices calibrated against separate reference bars, so the disagreement traces back to the standards themselves

pivots.stem: According to the professor, what did the party that revisited the Karnhout baseline find at the terminal marks?
settings: One of the buried marks had shifted, by enough to matter at the precision the work demanded
The marks themselves were sound, but stretches of the sight line between them had been built over
A boundary stone had been set over one mark by a landowner who took it for a property post
The marks were located without trouble, though their metal caps had been stripped in the meantime

pivots.stem: What does the professor suggest about the unpublished field books from the early campaigns?
settings: That parts of the series were split in an office move and now must be traced through two archives
That several books listed in the old inventory went out on loan decades ago and stayed out
That some observers' private notebooks, kept alongside the official ones, survive for a few campaigns
That the earliest books were recopied by clerks, and the originals may not have been kept

pivots.stem: Why does the professor bring up the instrument-maker Splinterveld?
settings: His delivery ledgers fix when each office received its apparatus, anchoring the chronology of the work
His letters show him adapting a design from abroad to the offices' habits before filling the orders
His price book shows how large a share of a campaign's budget the apparatus came to claim
He left the fullest description of the measuring routine, written out for the apprentice who took over his shop

pivots.stem: Why does the professor discuss the inspection reports from the Loonbeke school?
settings: They preserve the timetable of a school day, showing how much class time the exchanges took up
Their author disliked the routine, and his objections describe what it looked like in use
They show the school fitting the routine to a single room where several age groups sat together
They were written by a former pupil of Havermolen, which colors what they choose to report

pivots.stem: How does the professor respond to the claim that Tersagher devised the slate-exchange routine himself?
settings: She credits him with the written rules but thinks slates were being exchanged in village schools before him
She accepts it, arguing that the earlier routines described in reports were narrower than what he ran
She treats the question as open, since the record for the years before his tenure is thin
She thinks it was worked out jointly with his assistants, whose part later accounts let drop

pivots.stem: What does the professor say about the letters teachers sent to De Schoolbode concerning the routine?
settings: Most writers asked practical questions about marking, rather than debating the idea itself
The letters came disproportionately from schools in one district, for reasons the editors left unexplained
Several writers described changes they had made, some of which reversed the point of the original
Many letters were signed with initials, and a few have since been matched to known teachers

pivots.stem: What is the professor's main point about how the slate-exchange routine spread beyond Havermolen?
settings: It moved with junior teachers taking up first posts, which fits the patchy map of where it caught on
It spread through the columns of De Schoolbode, reaching many readers before they had seen a classroom use it
Much of the apparent spread was independent invention, since the routine answers a problem common to small schools
It spread through the summer refresher courses, where teachers from distant districts worked side by side

pivots.stem: What does the professor suggest about how the monitoring at Zandmere is likely to change?
settings: Surveys will be taken after storms as well as on the fixed dates, to catch changes the yearly visits miss
Ground parties will give way to flights, with the old beach profiles kept up at a few check sites
The routine measurements will pass to the harbor office, freeing the group for work farther offshore
The measured stretch will extend past the spit's tip, which the program has so far left out

pivots.stem: What is the professor's central explanation for why the design behaved differently at Zandmere than at Duivensgat?
settings: Sand arrives along the coast at Zandmere in pulses, and the spacing assumed a steady supply
The larger tide at Zandmere walks the waterline across a wider band than the layout was drawn to cover
The bed offshore lies mobile at depths that stay firm off Duivensgat, which told on the foundations
The works were built to the drawings but sited from an outdated chart, missing the channel they were meant to train

pivots.stem: Why does the professor show the photographs taken at the fishing hamlet of Kolverbaai?
settings: Taken for a family album, they happen to record the shore across decades the surveys skip
They show the sea at a road the older charts place well inland, fixing a floor on the rate of change
They record the boat sheds being moved landward twice, a measure of what the residents themselves saw
They catch the works under construction, at a stage the engineering files pass over

pivots.stem: What is the professor's assessment of the claim that the Duivensgat works starved the beaches downdrift of sand?
settings: He finds it persuasive for the nearest stretch, while laying the farther losses to the storms of that decade
He accepts it, adding that the effect was anticipated in a report the builders had set aside
He argues the beaches were losing sand beforehand, so the works at most hurried a change under way
He blames the dredging of the approach channel rather than the works, reversing the usual charge

pivots.stem: How does the professor judge the claim that Bruggelinck translated the Sedvael cycle from the Karvel version rather than the original?
settings: She thinks he leaned on the Karvel version for hard passages while working mainly from the original
She accepts it for the early books and thinks he learned the original language as the work went on
She rejects it, arguing the readings cited as proof were common knowledge among educated readers of his day
She thinks his source manuscript differed from the one modern editors use, which would produce the same readings

pivots.stem: What does the professor imply about the edition of the cycle now in preparation?
settings: That it will set the two translation lines side by side rather than choosing between them
That its commentary is being kept short so the volumes stay affordable for classroom use
That the editors have commissioned fresh versions of passages the older translators passed over
That its appearance has slipped while the editors argue over the ordering of the poems

pivots.stem: What is the professor's main point about why the two translation traditions of the cycle grew apart?
settings: Each tradition answered a different audience, one shaped by the stage and the other by the schoolroom
They drifted apart through revision, as each new editor corrected toward the habits of his own line
The split follows the verse form: one line kept the original meters, the other gave them up early
They parted over a handful of famous cruxes, and later differences radiate outward from those choices

pivots.stem: What does the professor say about the glossary found among Ostmaele's papers?
settings: It lists renderings he weighed and set aside, several now thought better than the ones he printed
It is written in another hand, suggesting he inherited a collaborator's working papers
It glosses words from dialects far from the poems' home region, a puzzle the professor leaves standing
It seems built for teaching rather than translating, with entries grouped by lesson instead of alphabet

pivots.stem: According to the professor, what did the surviving route books show about times on the Varn road?
settings: Times improved in steps that line up with changes of contractor rather than with work on the road
Winter runs came closer to the summer times than expected, apart from the stage with the ferry crossing
Southbound runs were consistently slower than northbound ones, a gap the books themselves do not explain
The posted schedule was met on most stages, with the recorded delays clustering at the sorting points

pivots.stem: Why does the professor bring up the innkeeper at Stukvoorde?
settings: His daybook logs the mail's passing times on its own account, apart from what the service recorded
His inn was the handover point where two services' riders met, the scene the professor keeps returning to
He petitioned for years to have the route brought past his door, and the file preserves both sides' arguments
His accounts show what riders spent along the way, costs the administration's ledgers pass over

pivots.stem: What does the professor imply about the neighboring administration's records of its own routes?
settings: That the relevant series survives, filed under a heading researchers seldom think to try
That much of it went for pulp in a paper drive, leaving that side of the correspondence thin
That it was kept in a form built for different questions, a sign of how differently the service ran
That a private collector holds the missing decades and has lately begun admitting researchers

pivots.stem: What is the professor's view of the claim that the neighboring service copied its way-bill audit from Grevelmark?
settings: He thinks the copying ran the other way, with Grevelmark taking up a procedure its neighbor was phasing out
He accepts it, pointing to early forms in the neighbor's files that still carry Grevelmark's printed heading
He argues both services took the audit from the customs houses, which had long checked their riders that way
He finds the resemblance shallow, a shared name covering procedures that worked quite differently in practice

pivots.stem: Why does the professor mention the beekeepers who worked the eastern heath?
settings: Their season diaries record good and poor flowering years, background the short spider surveys lack
One of them took the first specimens, well before the species received a formal description
Their sheds and hive stands turn out to shelter some of the densest web clusters on the heath
A hearing over their burning of old growth left testimony describing the former ground cover in rare detail

pivots.stem: What is the professor's central claim about how Dendermael's funnel-weaver came to occupy the two heaths?
settings: The heaths are remnants of a wider range, with the populations separated since the land between was drained
Spiderlings carried on autumn winds pass between the heaths often enough to keep the populations in touch
The eastern population descends from a small number of animals moved with cut turf within living memory
Both heaths were colonized separately from the coastal dunes, rather than either one from the other

pivots.stem: What is the professor's position on the claim that the western population is in decline?
settings: He accepts the counts but reads the change as a retreat into patches the survey routes undersample
He thinks the case is open either way, since the run of comparable counts is still short
He takes the decline as real and ties it to the maturing pine plantings along the heath's margin
He suspects the earlier counts were swollen by a look-alike species, so part of the drop is on paper

pivots.stem: According to the professor, what did the paired surveys show about where the webs sit on the two heaths?
settings: Eastern webs cluster in the oldest stands, while western webs favor the younger regrowth
On both heaths the webs keep to the south-facing slopes more closely than the literature had suggested
Webs sit lower in the vegetation in the east, which the team puts down to the more exposed ground
Western web sites turn over from year to year, while eastern sites stay in use season after season

pivots.stem: What does the professor imply the team plans for the next round of coring?
settings: Core the chain of small bogs lying between the two sites, adding intermediate points to the picture
Take paired cores at each bog, to learn how much the record shifts within a single site
Recore the original holes at a finer sampling interval, so the key levels can be dated more closely
Bank half of each new core unopened for later methods, a habit the professor says has paid off before

pivots.stem: How does the professor judge Bleyveld's argument that the velte pollen at Torsmoer drifted in from distant fields rather than nearby plots?
settings: She rejects it on the strength of the signal, which she finds too pronounced for a distant source
She accepts it for the lowest levels, while reading the later rise as growing near the bog itself
She accepts it, and takes the curve as tracking the crop's fortunes in districts well beyond the bog
She argues the pollen came in with harvested plants brought to the bog's edge for steeping, a third possibility

pivots.stem: What does the professor say the comparison of the two cores showed about the bogs themselves?
settings: Torsmoer's peat built up faster, so its record spreads the same centuries across a greater depth
Vennebroek's record holds a gap where the surface once dried, spanning a stretch the team had hoped to compare
The two bogs began forming at different times, though their upper sections run broadly in parallel
Thin bands of washed-in silt appear in both cores at what look to be matching levels

pivots.stem: Why does the professor bring in the dyers' guild books from Iselwaert?
settings: Their price entries put the plant's trade into years and seasons, a calendar the cores cannot supply
They record the guild trying substitutes during shortages, an episode the professor circles back to
A wage dispute in them names the workers who handled the plant, people otherwise missing from the record
They settle the plant's identity and spelling, which the older botanical literature had confused
